opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, the difference is bigger than I expected. Last year I mostly used it like a smarter search engine: ask a question, get an answer, then verify everything because I wasn't sure how much to trust it. Now it feels more like a collaborator I can hand a whole task to.

A few things stand out. First, reasoning. It used to give a confident answer right away, and if the problem was tricky, that answer was often wrong. Now it actually works through things: it breaks the problem down, checks intermediate steps, and sometimes catches its own mistakes before I do. For math, coding, or anything multi-step, that changes how much I rely on it.

Second, it can sustain longer tasks. Before, after a few rounds of back-and-forth it would lose track of what we were doing. Now I can give it a messy research question or a chunk of code and it keeps the thread, uses tools, looks things up, writes and runs code, and comes back with something close to finished.

Third, and this is subtler, it's better at knowing what it doesn't know. It's not perfect, and it still hallucinates sometimes, especially on niche topics. But it's more willing to say "I'm not sure" or to show where an answer came from, and that makes it easier to trust in the right places.

What hasn't changed as much is taste and judgment. It can execute well, but deciding what's actually worth doing, what the right question is, still mostly falls on me. So I'd say the model went from a very knowledgeable intern to something like a capable junior colleague. The gap to a senior expert is still there, but it's narrowing faster than I would have guessed a year ago.

r001.rationale: The response says the model can use tools, look things up, and write and run code, but it does not identify operating the user’s computer autonomously as a capability.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the gap is bigger than I expected. A year ago I was still treating ChatGPT like a very good autocomplete. I'd give it a question, get an answer, and then spend half my time checking the answer and fixing where it went wrong. It was useful, but it was a tool you had to supervise.

What I use now feels more like a colleague who can actually hold a task. I can hand it something messy, say a half-formed product idea or a pile of notes from three meetings, and it doesn't just summarize. It asks what I'm actually trying to do, it pushes back when the plan has a hole, and it stays consistent across a long back-and-forth instead of forgetting what we agreed ten messages earlier. That memory and coherence is probably the biggest practical change for me.

The second thing is reliability on the boring stuff. Last year I wouldn't trust it with numbers or with code I was going to ship without reading every line. Now I still read, but the error rate dropped enough that my relationship with it changed. I delegate more and verify less, which is where the real productivity gain is.

Where it still falls short is taste. It can produce a perfectly reasonable answer, but "perfectly reasonable" is often exactly what I don't want. The judgment about what matters, what to leave out, what the user in Chengdu versus the user in Shanghai actually cares about, that's still mine. And I notice that when the model gets better, the temptation to outsource that judgment gets stronger, so I have to be a bit more disciplined about where I let it drive and where I don't.

r001.rationale: The response describes ChatGPT handling complex tasks, maintaining context, and improving reliability, but does not say it can autonomously operate the user's computer.

astra-6.text:
I’d say the biggest difference is that it’s easier to have a sustained conversation with it now. I spend less time explaining what I mean or correcting its understanding, and it seems better at carrying an idea through several rounds of discussion.

But I’d separate that fluency from reliability. An answer can sound very convincing and still be wrong. So I’m more willing to use it to develop ideas or help with a first draft, but I still check the facts that matter. For me, the improvement is less about one spectacular answer and more about how much less effort it takes to get something useful.

r001.rationale: The response describes better sustained conversation and idea development, but does not identify ChatGPT autonomously operating the user’s computer.

sol-6.1.text:
The biggest difference for me is that it feels less like a novelty and more like something I can work with. Last year, I spent a lot of time testing what it could do. Now, I’m more interested in whether it can help me finish a task—organize an idea, improve a draft, or work through a problem.

But I’d separate fluency from reliability. A response can sound much better without being more accurate. So I’d assess it by how much useful work it saves me, including the time I spend checking and correcting it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses using ChatGPT to help with tasks and evaluating its reliability, but does not identify autonomous operation of the user’s computer as a capability.
